Showing 8 of 8 entries. How a mount is selected: the mount and the mass it carries form a spring-mass system with a natural frequency. Isolation only begins once the disturbing frequency is more than about 1.4 times that natural frequency, and is worth having at a ratio of three or more — which is why a softer mount usually isolates better, and why a mount that is too stiff for its load does nothing at all. Give us the supported mass per mounting point and the running speed of the machine and we will size it. Which Mount Material Do I Need?

On a mount the compound is chosen for how it behaves under repeated load, not for what it resists chemically. Natural rubber is the default and the right answer most of the time; the others are what you move to when oil, heat or weather rules it out.

Polyisoprene, and the standard anti-vibration compound. The highest resilience and the best fatigue life of the eight, with the lowest dynamic-to-static stiffness ratio — which is the property that decides whether a mount isolates in service as well as it does on paper. Not for oil, fuel or sustained heat.

Polychloroprene. The answer when a mount has to survive weather, ozone and moderate oil at the same time — an exposed machine foot or an under-bonnet mount. Slightly stiffer and less resilient than natural rubber, and worth the trade when the mount is outdoors. Also the family we reach for when flame retardancy is specified.

Nitrile butadiene rubber. Specified where the mount sits in or near petroleum oil or hydraulic fluid, which natural rubber cannot take. Dynamic behaviour is a compromise against natural rubber, so specify it for the oil, not for the isolation.

Styrene butadiene rubber. Abrasion resistance at low cost, blended with natural rubber in buffers and stoppers where the part takes impact rather than isolating a running machine. Not for oil or fuel contact.

Ethylene propylene diene rubber. For mounts that live outdoors or near steam and coolant, with excellent weather and ozone resistance. Higher damping and lower resilience than natural rubber. Not for petroleum oils.

Ethylene acrylic elastomer. Our signature compound, supplied to Mahindra & Mahindra for engine and transmission applications. Specified for a mount that has to hold its properties where oil, heat and ozone act together and neither natural rubber nor nitrile will last.

Fluorocarbon rubber. High cost, high damping loss and low resilience, so it is rarely specified for vibration isolation — it appears here because we mould it, and because a mount that is really a chemical-service block sometimes needs it.

Vinyl methyl silicone, the widest service range of the eight. Poor tear and fatigue resistance, and a bonded mount in silicone tends to fail at the bond line, so it is rarely specified for vibration isolation — use it for a static high-temperature pad rather than a running mount.
